abstract: Background: Tricuspid chordae play an important role in valve function. Unfortunately, they are poorly visible in clinical imaging and their mechanical properties cannot be measured noninvasively. This lack of data on chordal structure and properties limits our understanding of the tricuspid valve in general and efforts to model the valve in particular. Objectives: Our primary objective was to quantify chordal insertion patterns, structure, and mechanical properties. Our secondary objective was to test whether chordal structure and properties differed between control hearts and hearts with heart failure. Methods: We mapped chordal insertions in 25 excised human valves, measured the cross-sectional areas of 281 specimens, and conducted uniaxial tensile tests on 265 specimens from 12 of the 25 valves (eight control and four heart failure). We used mixed-effects models to assess the influence of heart failure and anatomical position. Finally, we used a hierarchical Bayesian model to represent area-dependent Ogden material parameters. Results: We found that chordal insertion density was highest at the free edge (p < 0.001), and lowest in the anterior leaflet (p < 0.001). Median cross-sectional area was 0.223 mm2, with anterior chordae the largest (p < 0.001) and septal the smallest (p < 0.001). A 10% increase in cross-sectional area was associated with 5.3% and 3.3% decreases in toe and calf stiffness, respectively. Heart failure was not associated with larger areas or higher stiffness. Conclusions: Human chordal geometry and material behavior varied with location and size. These openly shared data support assigning chordal insertions, sizes, and material properties in tricuspid valve models.
